implementation_notes: Guava's RateLimiter is the classic Java realization: RateLimiter.create(permitsPerSecond) distributes permits smoothly - when the rate is exceeded it releases one permit every 1/rate seconds - acquire() blocks until a permit is granted and returns the time slept, and tryAcquire() (optionally with a timeout) is the non-blocking shed path. It is safe for concurrent use by all threads but explicitly guarantees no fairness, and it models rate, not concurrency - the javadoc contrasts it with Semaphore and Little's law. A request may acquire several permits (acquire(packet.length)) to meter cost, but the charge falls on the next request, not the current one.
pitfalls: acquire() blocks the calling thread; on a bounded request pool a saturated limiter converts refusals into thread starvation and timeouts.
setRate does not wake threads already waiting, so the new rate only affects subsequent acquisitions.
The class carries Guava's @Beta annotation and its state is per JVM, never distributed.
Acquiring several permits at once throttles the next request rather than the current one - cost metering surprises callers expecting immediate feedback.

variants.name: Resilience4j RateLimiter (permissions per refresh cycle)
variants.implementation_notes: Resilience4j models the limit as permissions that refresh every limitRefreshPeriod: each cycle grants limitForPeriod permissions, AtomicRateLimiter keeps that state in an AtomicReference (SemaphoreBasedRateLimiter refreshes via a scheduler instead), and timeoutDuration decides whether an over-limit caller waits or is refused immediately with RequestNotPermitted. Decorators wrap Callable, Supplier, Runnable, Consumer or CompletionStage, the registry names and shares limiters, events expose successful and failed acquisitions, and changeLimitForPeriod tunes the rate at runtime - choose it when the limiter is one policy in a resilience stack alongside circuit breakers, retries and bulkheads.
pitfalls: Permissions refresh in cycles, so a caller can spend the whole allowance at a cycle boundary - burstier than Guava's smooth distribution.
The default timeoutDuration is 5 seconds: over-limit callers wait rather than fail unless it is set to ZERO deliberately.
Each limiter instance holds its own state; a limiter created per request or per thread never limits anything.
RequestNotPermitted is a runtime exception and must be mapped to 429/503 at the edge instead of surfacing as a 500.
